Market towns were the small towns of England and Wales that held a regular weekly market, by royal charter or old custom. Between about 1500 and 1640 there were some 800 of them, each serving a ring of villages, and Fernand Braudel uses them as his example of the plain, open market at the base of every economy.

Most market rights had been granted in the Middle Ages. The market was held on a fixed day in a square or a widened street, often with a market cross or covered hall. A farmer could walk there and back in a day, so towns were spaced a few miles apart, and each served a few thousand people.

What happened there:

  • Farmers sold grain, livestock, butter and cheese to townsfolk and to dealers.
  • Craftsmen and shopkeepers sold tools, cloth and salt to the villagers.
  • Officials checked weights, measures and prices, and tolls were paid to the lord of the market.

The open market was public and watched. In Braudel's scheme it is the transparent bottom layer of exchange, where prices were visible and competition was real. Above it, from the 1500s, more trade moved into private dealing, at inns and farms, by middlemen buying ahead of the market. That higher layer of large merchants and financiers, seen at Antwerp and Amsterdam, is what he calls capitalism.

The towns grew with the population and the London food trade, and the agricultural revolution that followed sold through them too. Many English towns still hold their market on the same day of the week.
